evidence.label: Continuum Coulomb hardness with binary nuclear charges
QMA-hardness of continuum Coulomb energy with unit nuclear charges

headline: Proves that estimating a molecule's exact electronic ground energy, from nuclear positions alone, is QMA-hard.
scope: Clamped nuclei at rational positions, Coulomb forces only, full spinful continuum of electron states; binary-coded charges, or all charges equal to one.
plain: Chemists want the lowest energy of the electrons in a molecule with fixed nuclei. Earlier hardness results needed a supplied set of orbitals or designed magnetic fields. These two papers prove the exact problem stays hard with only point nuclei as input, even when every nucleus has charge one. Lean checks both hardness statements; it says nothing about how good specific chemistry methods are.
doesNot: This does not show the problem belongs to QMA, that typical real molecules are hard, or that any particular chemistry method fails.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: O'Gorman, Irani, Whitfield and Fefferman, QMA-completeness of electronic structure in a supplied finite basis
scorecard.significanceWhy: It removes the supplied-basis and designed-potential assumptions from hardness results for the electronic structure problem.

explanation:
Start with one proton and one electron, a hydrogen atom. Its lowest electronic energy is −1/2 in atomic units, the hartree. Now pose a yes-or-no question with two thresholds, a = −0.4 and b = 0.6. Is the lowest energy at most a, or at least b? For hydrogen the answer is clearly yes, since −0.5 is below −0.4.

The general problem lists nuclei at fixed points with their charges, and a number of electrons. The electrons feel only Coulomb forces: attraction to the nuclei and repulsion from each other. The lowest energy E₀ is taken over every allowed electron state in ordinary three-dimensional space, with spin. A YES instance has E₀ ≤ a; a NO instance has E₀ ≥ b. The thresholds are promised to be far enough apart.

QMA is the quantum version of NP. A problem is in QMA when a quantum computer can check a proposed quantum state as evidence. A problem is QMA-hard when every QMA problem converts to it by an efficient classical recipe. So a fast general method for a QMA-hard problem would give fast methods for all of QMA.

Earlier results changed the question. O'Gorman, Irani, Whitfield and Fefferman proved QMA-completeness in a supplied finite basis of orbitals[3]. Schuch and Verstraete used designed potentials and local magnetic fields[4]. The obstacle is the continuum. Restricting to orbitals gives an upper bound on the energy. A NO answer needs a lower bound over every state outside those orbitals as well[5].

The first paper proves hardness when positive integer charges are written in binary[1]. The charges may then be exponentially large, but every output has polynomial length[8]. The second paper proves hardness when every nucleus has charge one[2]. Its recipe outputs polynomially many nuclei and electrons, with thresholds at least one hartree apart[9]. No orbital basis, magnetic field or extra potential is given[10]. The papers do not claim the problem lies in QMA[6].

The hardness is worst case. It says some carefully built arrangements of nuclei are hard. It does not say typical molecules are hard. The gap between thresholds is a precision promise, not an energy gap in the molecule[7].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal proofs of both hardness statements as given in the papers. They cover binary charges and unit charges, both over the full spinful continuum. These statements rely on a standard QMA-hard spin problem as their starting point. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid. Lean covers both hardness statements; the result is worst-case and makes no claim about typical molecules or QMA membership. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The lowest possible energy of the electrons for fixed positions of the nuclei.
Nuclei held fixed at given points, so only the electrons move.
The atomic unit of energy; a hydrogen atom's ground energy is −1/2 hartree.
All electron wave functions in ordinary space, not only those built from a chosen list of orbitals.
A fixed, finite list of one-electron shapes used to approximate the electrons' state.
Quantum Merlin-Arthur: problems whose YES answers a quantum computer can check from a quantum proof state.
At least as hard as every QMA problem, under an efficient classical conversion.
A yes-or-no question where inputs are guaranteed to fall clearly on one side of a gap.
